A singer has ten minutes left and three songs remaining. Panic begins. The tempo becomes slightly faster. The introduction is rushed. The instrumentalist barely completes one phrase before the next section begins. The singer starts thinking about finishing rather than communicating. The audience may not know why the performance suddenly feels uncomfortable, but they can feel it. The result may be that all three songs are completed—but none is truly experienced. Sometimes it is better to deliver two songs meaningfully than three songs mechanically. Professional time management means making intelligent adjustments. If time is running out, shorten the introduction. Remove an unnecessary repetition. Move directly into the next section. Drop a song if appropriate. Simplify the transition. Don’t sacrifice musical quality merely to say, “We completed the list.” Time management is not about squeezing everything into the available space but making the available space meaningful. In my work as a music instructor and mentor, I encourage performers to rehearse time variations. Don’t only practise the 45-minute version. Practise what happens if you suddenly have 35 minutes—or 50minutes.
